t.naurzum state nature reserve nsnr eco co:
In the steppes of northern Kazakhstan, in the Kostanay region, islands of pine forest rise out of the open grassland like a mirage, and between them lie shallow lakes full of birds. The Naurzum State Nature Reserve is one of the two parts of Saryarka – Steppe and Lakes of Northern Kazakhstan, listed by UNESCO in 2008 together with the Korgalzhyn reserve far to the east.

The lakes are vital stopover points for birds migrating between Africa, Europe and Asia and the breeding grounds of the Siberian tundra. In spring and autumn, huge flocks of geese, ducks and waders gather here, including rare species such as the white-tailed eagle, the imperial eagle and the Siberian white crane. The steppes are also home to marmots, wolves, foxes and saiga antelope, whose populations have been recovering after dramatic declines.

Visiting the reserve usually requires permission and a guide from the reserve administration, as access to the core areas is strictly controlled. The reserve has a visitor centre and organises tours to observation points and trails. The surrounding area is sparsely populated, with small villages, farms and enormous fields of wheat.

The riding here is about space and distance. The roads across the steppe are long and straight, often in poor condition, with potholes, gravel sections and dust, and tracks across the grassland can become impassable after rain. Wind is constant and can be strong. Distances between settlements are great, and services are limited, so plan carefully. Summers are hot and dry, winters bitterly cold with snowstorms; late spring, when the steppe is green and flowering, and early autumn, during the bird migration, are the best times to visit.

There are no large towns nearby. Karamendy, the village near the reserve headquarters, has basic shops, and Kostanay, the regional capital, has full services but is a long way off. Fuel stations are few, so fill up whenever you can and carry extra fuel, water and food. In the villages, Kazakh hospitality means you may be offered tea, bread and perhaps kumys, fermented mare's milk, or beshbarmak, the national dish of boiled meat and noodles. Watching the sun set over the steppe, with flocks of birds flying over the lakes, is an experience of great peace.
t.historic quarter of the city of colonia:
The ferry from Buenos Aires crosses the muddy, brown Rio de la Plata in about an hour, and when you arrive in Colonia del Sacramento, the city seems to have been kept in a jar. The Portuguese founded it in 1680 as a smuggling base to rival Spanish Buenos Aires on the opposite shore, and for the next century it was fought over by Portugal and Spain, passing from hand to hand. The old quarter on the peninsula is the result, with cobbled streets, low whitewashed houses with tiled roofs, and a mix of Portuguese and Spanish colonial styles. It was listed by UNESCO in 1995.

The best way to see it is on foot, and the sights are close together. The Calle de los Suspiros, the street of sighs, is a narrow lane of old houses that is the most photographed corner, and the lighthouse, built in the nineteenth century on the ruins of a convent, gives a view over the rooftops and the river. At sunset, the sky goes pink over the wide water, and people gather along the waterfront for a drink. The town's vintage cars, left parked as decoration among the flower beds, add to the nostalgia, and there is a quiet, unhurried feel even in high season.

The riding in Uruguay is easy and flat. Route 1 runs along the coast toward Montevideo, about 180 kilometres away, through farmland, cattle country and small towns, and is a good road with moderate traffic. Wind off the river can be strong, and in the summer months the roads are busy at weekends. The riding is relaxed rather than thrilling, and it suits an unhurried day, with a stop for a chivito, the local steak sandwich piled with egg, ham and cheese, and a few sips of mate if someone offers you some.

Colonia del Sacramento is a town of about twenty thousand people, with several fuel stations and plenty of restaurants. The best seasons are spring and autumn, with mild weather, and in summer it can be hot and humid. If you are coming from Buenos Aires, check the ferry rules for motorcycles and book ahead, and remember that your documents will be checked on arrival.
t.maison du docteur curutchet@-34.9,-57.9:
La Plata is a city with an unusual origin: it was planned from scratch in the 1880s as the new capital of Buenos Aires province, after the old city of Buenos Aires was made a federal district. Its founder, Dardo Rocha, commissioned a grid of streets with diagonals cut across it, and plazas every six blocks, a design inspired by Washington and Paris. The result is a calm, tree-lined place with a vast neo-Gothic cathedral and a university tradition.

Among its buildings is a famous small one, the house designed for Dr Pedro Domingo Curutchet by the Swiss-French architect Le Corbusier. It is the only house Le Corbusier built in the Americas, completed in the early 1950s, and is a compact, modernist work with a ramp running through the middle, a concrete frame, a brise-soleil of vertical fins and a small courtyard tree that rises through the interior. Dr Curutchet was a surgeon who wanted a home and a consulting room together, and the design separates them with a curious bridge between public and private life. The house is now a museum, run by the local architects' association, and it joined UNESCO's list of Le Corbusier's works in 2016.

For a rider, the interest here is a city run rather than an open road. The ride from Buenos Aires goes along the Autopista Buenos Aires-La Plata, a fast, busy motorway with tolls, and the city itself has wide avenues and moderate traffic. Surfaces are generally good, though cobbles and potholes appear on side streets, and the avenues are straight and flat. The pampas around are open and windy, with fields of soy and wheat and big skies. Spring and autumn are comfortable, summer is hot and humid.

La Plata has fuel, mechanics, hotels and plenty of cafes, and Berazategui further toward Buenos Aires has more. Parking near the house is limited, so check the visiting hours in advance. Try a medialuna, a small sweet croissant, with a cortado coffee, and look for the Sunday craft markets in the city's squares.
t.montevideo@-34.9,-56.2:
Montevideo is a city that faces the water and sits down beside it. A long waterfront road, the Rambla, runs for about twenty-two kilometres along the river Plate, and on any evening the whole city seems to be on it, with people walking, jogging, fishing or sitting with a thermos of hot water and a gourd of mate, the bitter herbal tea that Uruguayans carry everywhere. The river is so wide here that it looks like the sea, though it is brown with silt, and the Atlantic begins farther east.

The old city, Ciudad Vieja, sits on a small peninsula, a quiet grid of colonial buildings, art deco apartments and theatres, with the port market, Mercado del Puerto, at its edge. Inside the iron-framed market hall, grill restaurants cook beef, sausage and sweetbreads over open fires, and it is the place to understand Uruguay's relationship with meat. The Palacio Salvo, a tall, eccentric tower finished in 1928, dominates Independence Square. Spanish colonists founded the city in the 1720s as a military outpost against the Portuguese, and the rivalry shaped the early history of the region. Football is another passion, and the Estadio Centenario hosted the first World Cup final in 1930, won by Uruguay.

For riders, the coast road east is the highlight. From Montevideo, the Interbalnearia highway runs through a series of beach towns toward Punta del Este and on to the quieter beaches of Rocha, ending at Cabo Polonio, a fishing village on a sandy headland with no road access, where visitors travel by 4x4 across the dunes. The road itself is flat, smooth and busy near the capital, and relaxed beyond. Winds off the Atlantic can be strong, and sudden storms called pamperos sweep up from the south. Summer, from December to February, brings crowds to the beaches, and spring and autumn are quieter.

Fuel is easy to find in the city and along the coast, and tolls are charged on the main highway, so carry cash or check how to pay for a motorbike. In the evening, Candombe drums echo through some neighbourhoods, a tradition of Afro-Uruguayan music that is a main part of the carnival, which locals say is the longest in the world.
t.buenos aires@-34.6,-58.4:
Buenos Aires is the capital that looks across a river wide enough to be mistaken for the sea. The Río de la Plata is brown, shallow and enormous, and the city that sits on its western shore has always seemed to face outward, toward Europe. Pedro de Mendoza first tried to found a settlement in 1536 and failed, and Juan de Garay refounded it in 1580. Since then the port has grown into one of the great cities of the southern hemisphere, with about thirteen million people in its wider area, wide avenues designed on a Parisian scale, and cafés that keep a table for you all afternoon.

Start with the middle. The Plaza de Mayo holds the pink Casa Rosada, the cathedral and the weekly circle of the mothers whose children disappeared under the military dictatorship, a quiet and moving ritual. San Telmo has cobbled streets, antique shops and a Sunday market. La Boca has painted metal houses and a football stadium that shakes when the crowd sings. Recoleta has a cemetery of ornate marble tombs that is a city in itself. Avenida 9 de Julio is among the widest streets in the world, and crossing it takes more than one set of lights. Tango is the music of the neighbourhoods, and you will hear it in bars as often as in shows.

For a rider the city is a challenge in the best and worst senses. Traffic is intense, motorcycles weave through lanes with little ceremony, and rain makes the old tramlines and painted markings slick. Leaving is easier by motorway: the Panamericana to the north, the autopista to La Plata in the south, or the roads west to the pampas, which run flat and straight for hours through cattle country. Tolls are common and cash helps. This is also the starting point for the ride to Fray Bentos in Uruguay, crossing the river by a bridge far upstream or by ferry, so check border papers and insurance in advance.

Fuel is everywhere and usually easy to buy. Eat steak at least once, preferably in a plain parrilla with checked tablecloths, and drink maté with locals if you are offered it. Spring and autumn are the best seasons. Summers are sticky, and winters are mild but damp. Do not leave the bike on the street overnight in some neighbourhoods; ask your hotel about secure parking.
t.piriapolis@-34.9,-55.3:
Piriápolis was invented. In the 1890s an energetic Uruguayan businessman named Francisco Piria bought a stretch of empty coast and dunes below a pair of granite hills, and set about building a seaside resort from nothing, with a hotel, a promenade, a castle for himself and a mineral-water business. The town grew from that dream, and its old-fashioned seafront still wears a faintly European, Belle Époque air, with a long curving promenade, a pier, and the grand Hotel Argentino, built in 1930 and still standing on the front.

The town of about eight thousand people sits at the foot of Cerro Pan de Azúcar, a conical granite hill that is among the highest points in the southeast, and the Cerro del Toro rises to the east. Piria's castle, a quirky stone building with turrets, is on the hillside, and a chairlift runs up Cerro San Antonio for views over the beach and the open water of the Río de la Plata. The sea here is calm and brown-green, the estuary rather than the open ocean, and sunsets glow behind the hills.

For a rider, Piriápolis is the start of the road east. Ruta 10 and Ruta 93, the Interbalnearia, run along the coast to Punta del Este and beyond, while inland roads climb through the sierras to Pan de Azúcar and Minas, gentle, curving lanes through eucalyptus and open pasture. The surface is generally good, with some rough patches, and the traffic is light outside summer. Wind off the water can be strong, and mornings are often misty. In January, the town is crowded with Argentine and Uruguayan holidaymakers, and rooms are scarce.

Fuel is easy in town, and the seafront has bakeries and restaurants that serve grilled fish and chivito, the national steak sandwich. Winter is quiet and mild, with empty promenades and cold wind. Spring and autumn are the best months, with clear light and soft temperatures. Take the chairlift if the weather is clear, and eat something fried by the water, then leave early for the long coastal run to Cabo Polonio, where the road narrows and the country empties out.
t.the work of engineer eladio dieste churc:
A concrete wave stands beside the beach road in Atlántida, and it is a church. The Iglesia de Cristo Obrero y Nuestra Señora de Lourdes, in the Estación Atlántida district, was designed by the Uruguayan engineer Eladio Dieste and finished in 1960. It is made entirely of brick, and its undulating walls ripple like fabric, rising to a sinuous roofline that seems to defy the material. Dieste used a technique he called reinforced ceramic, which allowed thin brick shells to span huge spaces with almost no thickness. The result is light, strong and beautiful, and in 2021 UNESCO added the church to the World Heritage list.

Inside, the effect is even better. Light enters through slender gaps in the wall and spills down the curving brick, and the whole interior feels like a calm cave of warm red-orange. There is no decoration to speak of, only the geometry. It is a working parish church, so visiting hours are limited and respect for services is expected. Check ahead if you want to go inside.

The riding along the coast east of Montevideo is easy. The Interbalnearia, the main coastal highway, links a string of beach resorts, among them Atlántida, Las Toscas and La Floresta, all low-rise and a little faded, with eucalyptus and pine groves behind the dunes. The water of the Río de la Plata is brown and wide, more like a sea than a river, and the beaches are long and sandy. Summer, from December to February, is busy and warm, and the road fills with beach traffic at weekends; off season it is quiet and breezy.

Pando, about eighteen kilometres inland, is the nearest bigger town and has fuel and shops, though Atlántida itself has stations and plenty of places to eat. Try a chivito, the steak sandwich that is Uruguay's national snack, and drink mate like the locals. Watch for sandy patches on the beach roads and for winds off the river. A late afternoon visit, when the sun lights the brick, is the best.
t.fray bentos industrial landscape@-33.1,-:
Fray Bentos is a small city on the east bank of the Río Uruguay, and its fame comes from a corned-beef tin. In 1865, a company built a factory here to make Liebig's Extract of Meat, a concentrate of beef boiled down from the enormous herds of the pampas, and the plant grew into a giant that shipped meat products around the world. Later a British-owned company took it over, and the brand Fray Bentos, still sold on supermarket shelves as tinned pies in Britain, was born. The factory closed in the late 1970s, and today the whole complex, with its brick sheds, chimney and workers' houses, is a museum, listed by UNESCO in 2015 as an industrial landscape.

The setting is the broad brown river, nearly wide enough to look like a sea. On the Argentine shore, the city of Gualeguaychú is about twenty kilometres away, and the two countries are linked by the General San Martín bridge. In the 2000s, a pulp mill built near Fray Bentos led to a long dispute, when Argentine protesters blocked the bridge for years, so the crossing has some local memory. The countryside is rolling grassland, with cattle, eucalyptus and the occasional ombú tree.

A day ride from Buenos Aires means a long run on flat roads, through the Entre Ríos farmland, over the river and into Uruguay, so the main effort is distance. The roads are generally good, straight and wide, with truck traffic and speed control, and crosswinds from the river can be strong. Border formalities take time, requiring passports, vehicle papers and sometimes an insurance check, so allow an hour or more. In summer, the heat is heavy and thunderstorms build quickly in the afternoon. Spring and autumn are more comfortable.

Practically, Fray Bentos has fuel stations, supermarkets and small restaurants, and the riverfront has a promenade and cafes. Local food includes grilled beef, chivito sandwiches and the sweet dulce de leche, and mate is carried everywhere in a thermos. The museum is open most days and takes a couple of hours. Parking for motorbikes is easy, and the old town is compact. Fill up before leaving, because rural stretches have few stations.
t.deer lake newfoundland@49.2,-57.4:
Deer Lake is where most people's Newfoundland begins or ends, since its small airport takes the jets from Toronto and Halifax, and it is also where the Viking Trail leaves the Trans-Canada Highway and turns north. The town sits at the foot of the lake from which it takes its name, at the mouth of the Humber River, with the dark hills of the Long Range rising behind and spruce forest everywhere you look. It is a plain, practical place, and that is how you want it to be at the start of a long run north.

Route 430, the Viking Trail, is the road that matters. It runs about four hundred kilometres up the west coast of the island's Great Northern Peninsula to the tip, passing Gros Morne National Park, with its fjords, the stark orange plateau of the Tablelands and a mountain that looks like a tilted table, and ending near L'Anse aux Meadows, where Norse settlers camped about a thousand years ago, the only confirmed Viking site in North America. Both parks are World Heritage sites. The road itself is a calm, smooth ribbon, mostly straight with gentle bends and occasional climbs, between the sea on one side and bog and forest on the other.

Be honest about the hazard: moose. Newfoundland has a very large moose population, introduced in 1904, and collisions are frequent, particularly at dawn and dusk, so ride at modest speeds and scan the verges constantly. Weather is the other variable, with fog, wind and cold rain common even in summer, and a few days of clear light a real prize. Pack a waterproof layer and warm gloves in July.

Deer Lake has more than four thousand people and decent services, including fuel, supermarkets, motels and a couple of diners, so stock up before heading north. Beyond Corner Brook and Deer Lake, the towns shrink quickly and stations are widely spaced, and in the north some close early. Never let the tank get low.

Food on the road is simple and good: cod, fish and chips, toutons, which are fried bread dough eaten with molasses, and partridgeberry jam. Ask what the local specialty is, and you will usually get an honest answer.
t.gros morne@49.7,-57.8:
Gros Morne is the second-highest mountain in Newfoundland, a bald dome of about eight hundred metres, but the name is also used for the whole national park that surrounds it on the island's west coast, and the park is the point. UNESCO made it a World Heritage Site in 1987, largely because of its geology: here the deep rocks of the Earth's mantle have been pushed up and exposed, and you can see the process that is usually hidden miles below the surface. The Tablelands, a flat-topped massif of orange-brown rock that looks more like Mars than Canada, are the best example, and almost nothing grows on them because the rock is toxic to most plants.

The Viking Trail, Route 430, which runs north along the coast to L'Anse aux Meadows, passes through the park and is the main road for riders. It is smooth and wide, with long views of the sea on one side and the mountains on the other, and it dips in and out of fishing villages with brightly painted houses. Bonne Bay, a fjord-like arm of the sea cut into the park, is crossed by the road, and Rocky Harbour and Norris Point on its shores have fuel, cafes and places to sleep. The fuel is the part worth planning, since distances on the island are large and stations in the park are few. Deer Lake, to the south, has the airport and a wider choice of services.

Weather is a character of its own. Fog rolls in from the Atlantic with no warning, wind can be fierce on the headlands, and rain showers sweep through even in summer, so the layers go on and off through the day. Moose were introduced to Newfoundland in the nineteenth century and now number in the hundreds of thousands. They stand in the road and walk out from the trees, particularly at dawn and dusk, and a collision is serious, so riding at night is unwise.

A boat trip on Western Brook Pond, a freshwater fjord cut off from the sea and enclosed by cliffs that rise six hundred metres, is among the best excursions, reached by a walk of about three kilometres over a boggy path. The fishing villages serve cod, mussels and lobster, and local bakeries sell partridgeberry jam and bread. The riding season is short, from about June to September, and the best months are July and August.
t.naurzum state nature reserve nsnr tersek:
In the steppe of northern Kazakhstan, the Naurzum reserve covers a patch of country that, from a distance, looks like nothing and, from close up, turns out to be a world of its own. It lies in the Kostanay region, in the dry heart of the Turgay plains, and is made of grassland, salt lakes, birch groves and, remarkably, a strip of old pine forest called Naurzum Karagai that survives here, far south of the main taiga. Tersek is one of the separate sectors of the reserve. Together with Korgalzhyn it forms a UNESCO site, the steppe and lakes of northern Kazakhstan, inscribed in 2008.

The importance of the place lies in its birds. The lakes and wetlands of the Kazakh steppe stand on a major migratory route between Africa, South Asia and Siberia, and in spring and autumn they fill with ducks, geese, swans and waders. Rare species such as the Dalmatian pelican, the steppe eagle and the demoiselle crane have been recorded in the region, and the grasslands support the saiga antelope, a strange-nosed animal that once roamed in millions and has made a cautious comeback. In spring the steppe is covered in tulips and feather grass, and the whole landscape ripples in the wind.

This is a remote area, and a ride here has more in common with an expedition than a casual tour. The main roads across the steppe are long and straight, with surfaces that vary widely, and the distances between settlements are great. Tracks into the reserve are sandy or muddy, and the reserve itself requires permission to enter, so it is wise to arrange it in advance with the administration. Summer brings extreme heat and swarms of mosquitoes near the lakes, and winters are bitterly cold, with blizzards and temperatures far below freezing. May and early June, when the steppe is green and the birds are nesting, are the best time.

There are no towns on the map near this point, so plan carefully. Fill the tank at the regional centres, carry extra fuel, water, food and a way to repair a puncture, and let someone know your route. Village shops sell basic supplies, and hospitality in the steppe is a matter of pride, with tea, bread and sour milk offered to travellers.
t.naurzum state nature reserve nsnr main a:
Kazakhstan is mostly steppe, and this is the northern part of it, an enormous open country of feather grass, lakes and wind. The Naurzum reserve, in the Kostanay region, protects a patch of that landscape, together with an oddity that surprises everyone, an island of ancient pine forest sitting in the steppe. The pines grow on sandy ground left by an old river, and they form a relict stand that survived when the climate changed. Together with the nearby Korgalzhyn reserve it was recognised by UNESCO as the Saryarka, the Steppe and Lakes of Northern Kazakhstan, and the lakes are a major stopover for migratory birds on the flyway from Africa and India to Siberia.

In spring and autumn the air is full of wings. Flamingos wade in the salty shallows, Dalmatian pelicans cruise past, and cranes, geese, swans and ducks arrive by the hundreds of thousands. Steppe eagles and other raptors sit on the posts, and the rare saiga antelope, with its bulbous nose, has been recovering in the wider region. In May the steppe is covered in tulips, and in July it dries to gold. The smell of wormwood in the heat is something you do not forget.

The roads in this region are long, flat and empty, with big skies and a feeling of progress without arrival. The main highways are paved, though maintenance varies, and the access roads into the reserve are gravel and dirt, which become impossible after heavy rain or snowmelt. Wind can be fierce, and temperatures swing from forty degrees in July to minus thirty in January, so plan for late spring or early autumn. Distances are large, and you should assume that nothing will be open between villages.

Reserves in Kazakhstan generally require an entrance permit or a registered guide, and a visit is easiest if arranged through the park administration in advance. Mosquitoes are fierce near the lakes in summer. Villagers sell fish and dairy products at the roadside in season, and a bowl of fermented mare's milk is a traditional offer.
t.naurzum state nature reserve nsnr sypsyn:
The steppe at Naurzum is the kind of place where the horizon is a straight line in every direction. This is northern Kazakhstan, in Kostanay region, a flat country of feather grass, salt lakes and shimmering heat, and in the middle of it a protected area that holds one of the last stretches of unploughed steppe, together with a pine forest that has no right to be there. The reserve was listed by UNESCO as part of Saryarka, Steppe and Lakes of Northern Kazakhstan, in 2008.

What makes it special is the birdlife. Naurzum sits on the Central Asian flyway, and in spring and autumn huge numbers of migrating birds stop at the lakes, including flamingos at the southern edge of their range, pelicans, cranes and geese. Rare steppe species such as the Dalmatian pelican and the steppe eagle breed or pass through. If you like watching birds, May is a wonderful month, and the dawn chorus on the lake shores is loud.

For a rider, the interest is in distance and emptiness. Roads on the plain are sometimes tarmac that has seen better decades, and just as often gravel or dirt tracks that become impassable in wet weather. Wind is constant, strong and often sideways, and a fully loaded bike gets pushed around. In summer the heat is dry and serious, and in winter it is bitterly cold, with temperatures well below minus twenty. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons.

Fuel is the thing to plan. There is none at the reserve, and villages in this part of Kazakhstan may be far apart, so carry a reserve and fill up whenever you pass a station. The reserve is protected, and visits usually require registering with the staff and keeping to marked tracks. Go in with a plan, a full tank and enough water, and take time for the stillness, because the sky out here is enormous and the sunsets are slow.
t.esma museum and site of memory former cl:
This is not a place for tourists in the usual sense, and it is better to arrive knowing why. The ESMA, the Navy Mechanics School, is a complex of handsome neoclassical buildings in the Núñez district in the north of Buenos Aires, set in leafy grounds on the Avenida del Libertador. During the military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983 it was also one of the largest clandestine detention centres in the country. Thousands of people were held and tortured here, and most of them were killed, many thrown alive from aircraft into the Río de la Plata. Only a small number survived, and their testimony helped bring the junta's leaders to court.

After years of argument, the grounds were handed over in 2004 and turned into a museum and site of memory, with some of the buildings left deliberately bare, as evidence. UNESCO added it to the World Heritage list in 2023. The visit is intense and quiet. Guides take small groups through the Officers' Mess, the attic where prisoners were held and the basement, and they do not hurry or dramatise. The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo, who still march every Thursday in the centre of the city, are part of the story that is told here, and the name is spoken with respect by every porteño.

The ride is purely urban. From the centre or the southern suburbs, you take the Avenida del Libertador or the riverside Costanera, past parks, embassies, the racecourse at Palermo and wide, tree-lined avenues. Traffic is dense, drivers are quick, and motorbikes filter at speed, so keep your eyes up, and watch the paving, which is often cracked and slippery after rain. Parking a bike near the entrance is usually possible, and the area is calm and residential.

Fuel is easy in Buenos Aires, with stations on every major avenue, and Belgrano and Colegiales nearby offer cafes where you can sit afterwards. Give yourself some time to sit with it. A coffee and a medialuna in a corner bar, watching ordinary Buenos Aires roll past the window, helps you take in what you have seen and remember why it matters.
t.deer lake@49.2,-57.4:
Deer Lake is where western Newfoundland begins for most visitors, because it has the airport, a handful of motels, and the junction where the Viking Trail leaves the Trans-Canada Highway and heads north. About 4,600 people live here, there is fuel in town, and it is the last place with real choice before the long empty miles on Route 430. Treat it as the point to fill the tank, eat something warm, and check the sky.

The lake that gives the town its name is the broad lower end of the Humber River system, and the Humber itself is one of the great salmon rivers of the island. The valley is gentle and forested, with spruce and fir on the hills and patches of bog, and the road along it is quick and friendly, a good place to settle into the bike before the coast takes over. The surface on the main routes is serviceable rather than glossy, with frost heave and patched sections that come with a place where winter tries hard.

Newfoundland has its own rules for riders, and the first is moose. There are a great many on the island, they are enormous, and they step onto the road at dawn and dusk with no sense of drama. Plan your day so that you are not riding the long forested stretches in the half-light, and keep your speed within what you can stop in. The second rule is to carry a layer: even in high summer a wind off the Gulf of St. Lawrence can drop the temperature sharply, and fog can sit on the coast for days.

The ride from here is a story about the far end of the Great Northern Peninsula, where Norse seafarers built a small settlement about a thousand years ago at L'Anse aux Meadows, the only confirmed Viking site in North America and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1978. Between here and there lie Gros Morne, fishing coves painted in strong colours, and a lot of sky. Ask at a local counter about the day's weather and you will get an honest answer, usually delivered with a joke attached.
t.gros morne@49.6,-57.9:
Gros Morne is a national park and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the reason is under your wheels as much as in front of you. Here, on the west coast of Newfoundland, ancient ocean floor and a slice of the Earth's mantle were pushed up onto the continent when old continents collided. The result is the Tablelands, an orange-brown plateau of peridotite that looks like a piece of Mars dropped between green hills and a cold sea. Few plants tolerate the mineral chemistry, so the ground stays eerily bare.

The mountain that gives the park its name is a rounded 806-metre dome, and the rest of the scenery is on a grand scale too: Bonne Bay, a deep fjord-like inlet, cuts into the land, and inland lies Western Brook Pond, a freshwater fjord whose cliffs rise straight from the water. The villages around Bonne Bay, such as Rocky Harbour and Norris Point, are working fishing communities, and they are where you will find coffee, a bed, and most likely fuel; ask before you count on it late in the evening.

For a rider, the Viking Trail through here is relaxed and scenic more than technical. The bends are easy and the road follows the coast with the Gulf of St. Lawrence on one side and the Long Range Mountains on the other, so views turn up in long, generous sweeps. Wind can be serious on the exposed sections, and on cold days the sea fog drifts across the road and changes the ride completely. Moose are the main hazard, especially at dawn, dusk and in drizzle, so keep your speed honest and your eyes on the verges.

The people who settled this coast fished cod for centuries, and traces of that life show in the wooden stages, the stacked traps and the small churches. Before them, Indigenous peoples and Norse sailors passed through. Plan for the weather to be the dominant character: you may get one blue day, one grey day and one wet day, and the sensible response is to ride whatever you are given and stop at a bakery when the rain really sets in.

Montevideo is a city that faces the water and sits down beside it. A long waterfront road, the Rambla, runs for about twenty-two kilometres along the river Plate, and on any evening the whole city seems to be on it, with people walking, jogging, fishing or sitting with a thermos of hot water and a gourd of mate, the bitter herbal tea that Uruguayans carry everywhere. The river is so wide here that it looks like the sea, though it is brown with silt, and the Atlantic begins farther east.

The old city, Ciudad Vieja, sits on a small peninsula, a quiet grid of colonial buildings, art deco apartments and theatres, with the port market, Mercado del Puerto, at its edge. Inside the iron-framed market hall, grill restaurants cook beef, sausage and sweetbreads over open fires, and it is the place to understand Uruguay's relationship with meat. The Palacio Salvo, a tall, eccentric tower finished in 1928, dominates Independence Square. Spanish colonists founded the city in the 1720s as a military outpost against the Portuguese, and the rivalry shaped the early history of the region. Football is another passion, and the Estadio Centenario hosted the first World Cup final in 1930, won by Uruguay.

For riders, the coast road east is the highlight. From Montevideo, the Interbalnearia highway runs through a series of beach towns toward Punta del Este and on to the quieter beaches of Rocha, ending at Cabo Polonio, a fishing village on a sandy headland with no road access, where visitors travel by 4x4 across the dunes. The road itself is flat, smooth and busy near the capital, and relaxed beyond. Winds off the Atlantic can be strong, and sudden storms called pamperos sweep up from the south. Summer, from December to February, brings crowds to the beaches, and spring and autumn are quieter.

Fuel is easy to find in the city and along the coast, and tolls are charged on the main highway, so carry cash or check how to pay for a motorbike. In the evening, Candombe drums echo through some neighbourhoods, a tradition of Afro-Uruguayan music that is a main part of the carnival, which locals say is the longest in the world.
